links.comparator_used: No transparency (control) and narrative explanations with citations, in a 3-arm randomized experiment.
links.outcome: Tool-specific trust, global trust, and perceived information credibility
links.effect: tool-specific trust [F(2, 214) = 0.38, P = .68], global trust [F(2, 217) = 0.13, P = .88], perceived information credibility [F(2, 210) = 0.42, P = .66]
links.quote: Transparency did not influence tool-specific trust [F(2, 214) = 0.38, P = .68], global trust [F(2, 217) = 0.13, P = .88], or perceived information credibility [F(2, 210) = 0.42, P = .66].

links.comparator_used: No transparency control (AI diagnostic output without rationale); also numeric confidence scores
links.outcome: Trust, perceived credibility, confidence change, and behavioral influence
links.effect: Narrative explanations with citations did not shift trust (all P > .6 across transparency conditions). Confidence change was greater than with control (P = .024) and numeric confidence (P = .0051). Behavioral influence was lower in transparency conditions than control (P = .0006).
links.tradeoff: Confidence increased without a corresponding change in trust (a trust-confidence dissociation). Behavioral influence was lower than in the control group.
links.quote: Confidence increased following any AI assistance (+6.7%), but narrative explanations were associated with greater change in confidence compared with both control (P = .024) and numeric confidence (P = .0051).

design_hint: transparency features (confidence scores, narrative explanations with citations)
